newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Council set to authorize force for E. Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Council set to authorize force for E. Zaire.

text.p: As countries organised troops for an intervention force to prevent starvation in eastern Zaire, the U.N. Security Council was expected on Friday to authorise the mission for a maximum of four months.

A draft resolution, obtained by Reuters, would allow the force to use "all necessary means" to get food, water and medical supplies to more than a million Hutu refugees whose aid has been cut by fighting in the region. Canada will lead the operation.

But Canadian and U.S. officials have ruled out disarming militia blamed for discouraging Hutu refugees from returning to their homes in Rwanda or Burundi where minority Tutsis are running both governments.

The resolution says the operation, eventually expected to reach at least 10,000 troops, would "facilitate" the return of refugees. But the document -- as well as an accompanying letter to the council from Canada's U.N. ambassador Robert Fowler -- deliberately leaves vague how the troops would keep the extremists from re-establishing themselves.

The mission's humanitarian objectives were "not intended to interfere with the balance of military forces in the area nor to support the re-establishment of camps in which armed elements are able to operate," Fowler said in his letter, which was requested by the council before the resolution could be adopted.
The resolution also:
-- authorises the mission under Chapter VII of the U.N. Charter which allows the use of force.
-- ends the operation no later than March 31, as the United States had insisted.
-- calls for a "follow-on" force that U.N. officials said they had been planning under a U.N. command. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali is to submit his recommendations by Jan. 1.
-- says that costs for the new multinational force would be borne by participating nations but asks Boutros-Ghali to set up a fund for African states to help pay for their troops.
Although the troops will not be under a U.N. command, contributors have insisted they be authorised by the 15-seat Security Council to give them international legitimacy.

About 1.5 million refugees, mainly Hutus, fled Rwanda in 1994, fearing reprisals after the massacre of up to a million Tutsis and Hutu moderates. The eastern Zairean province of Kivu has remained politically tense since then, with a new war breaking out in September between Tutsi residents of Zaire and local Zairians, backed by Zaire's army.
Planning for the mission intensified at U.N. headquarters on Thursday with Canada's Lt.-Gen. Maurice Baril, who will command the force, meeting with miitary experts from various countries.

The way was cleared to deploy the force after the United States signalled on Wednesday it was prepared to join the operation with 1,000 troops in Zaire and up to 4,000 additional soldiers as backup in neighbouring countries.

But Canada's deputy foreign minister, Gordon Smith, did not play down the dangers involved. "There are enormous risks in this. No question about that (but) we think the risks are worth taking," he told a news conference.

Baril said the troops would take over the airfields in eastern Zairean towns of Goma and Bukavu with the United States securing Goma, which would also be his main headquarters. From there the troops would establish land corridors to bring in relief supplies and fan westward where many of the refugees fled.
Staging areas for the force will be established in Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda but diplomats said most of the troops would arrive at the Ugandan airport of Entebbe.
They said the initial force would include soldiers from the United States, Canada, Britain, France, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, South Africa and Senegal.
Other countries that may join later are Cameroon, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Egypt, Mali, Ireland, Brazil and Portugal. Norway and Finland may send human rights observers.

To induce refugees to return home, feeding areas will also be set up near the Rwandan and Burundi borders and human rights monitors may be increased in Rwanda from 110 to 300. In addition relief supplies, including seeds for planting, are to be delivered to Rwanda.
